content: Pokeweed, also referred to as poke, pokebush, pokeberry, pokeroot, polk salad, polk sallet, inkberry, or ombú, belongs to the genus Phytolacca. These are perennial plants native to regions such as North America, South America, East Asia, and New Zealand. Pokeweed contains toxic compounds, specifically phytolaccatoxin and phytolaccigenin, which are harmful to mammals. However, birds can consume the berries without adverse effects because the seeds, which have extremely hard outer shells, remain undigested and are excreted intact. Pokeweed plants typically grow to heights ranging from 1 to 10 feet. They feature single, alternate leaves that are pointed at the tips and have crinkled edges. The stems are often pink or red in color. The flowers are greenish-white and grow in elongated clusters at the ends of the stems, eventually developing into dark purple berries. A specific species, Phytolacca dioica (commonly known as ombú), grows as a tree in the pampas of South America and provides shade in the open grasslands. It is considered a cultural symbol of Argentina and the gaucho lifestyle. Uses of Pokeweed Young leaves of pokeweed can be boiled three times, with the water discarded after each boiling, to reduce the toxin levels. The resulting preparation is known as poke salit or poke salad and is sometimes commercially available. Despite this preparation method, many experts caution against consuming pokeweed, as residual toxins may still remain. Historically, poke salad has been a staple in Southern U.S. cuisine, even though medical professionals have raised concerns about its safety. The cultural significance of poke salad is reflected in the 1969 song Polk Salad Annie, written and performed by Tony Joe White and later covered by Elvis Presley. Pokeberry juice has been used in combination with other juices to make jelly, with some individuals believing it alleviates arthritis pain. Pokeweed has also been employed in homeopathic remedies for various conditions. Topical applications have been used to treat acne and other skin ailments, while internal use has been associated with treating tonsillitis, swollen glands, and even weight loss. Native Americans historically used grated pokeroot as a poultice to address breast inflammations and rashes. The berries of pokeweed produce a red ink or dye, which Native Americans once used to decorate horses. Notably, the Declaration of Independence of the United States was reportedly written using fermented pokeberry juice, which is why the plant is sometimes called inkberry. During the Civil War, letters written with pokeberry ink have survived, though the writing has turned brown over time. The red juice has also been used symbolically to represent blood, such as in anti-slavery protests by Benjamin Lay. Additionally, a rich brown dye can be created by fermenting the berries and soaking fabrics in the resulting liquid. Pokeweed is sometimes cultivated as an ornamental plant due to its visually appealing berries. Certain cultivars have been developed to produce larger fruit clusters. The plant also serves as a food source for the larvae of some Lepidoptera species, including the Giant Leopard Moth. Toxic Principles The primary toxic components of pokeweed are saponins, which are present in the berry juice and other parts of the plant. Additional toxic substances include the alkaloids phytolaccine and phytolaccotoxin, as well as a glycoprotein. If pokeweed is prepared as food, the water used for boiling must be discarded to reduce toxicity. Clinical Signs of Toxicity Ingesting non-lethal amounts of pokeweed, such as the shoots, may result in symptoms like retching or vomiting after a delay of two or more hours. These symptoms can progress to include difficulty breathing (dyspnea), excessive sweating, muscle spasms, severe diarrhea (often bloody), prostration, tremors, and, in some cases, convulsions. Consuming a fatal dose, which may include the roots, can lead to respiratory paralysis and other narcotic effects, ultimately resulting in death. Additional signs of toxicity include colic, diarrhea, respiratory failure, unsteadiness, inability to stand, and jerking movements of the legs. In livestock, toxicity may also cause a decrease in milk production.
